# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. horror movie masterpieces to watch this Halloween 🎃

**Score:** 46
**Body:** With Halloween coming up, I honestly don’t feel like going out much this year, so I thought: why not have an old-school horror movie marathon instead? 🎃👻

I’m looking for recommendations for genuinely creepy and unsettling horror movies. The kind that leave you feeling uneasy long after watching them and make it hard to sleep at night! 🩸🕯️

What are your best recommendations? I’m open to anything, especially hidden gems!

The Fog (1980)

Poltergeist (1982)

House on Haunted Hill (1959)

The Thing (1982)

## 4. Amazon prime video suggestions PLEASE

**Score:** 16
**Body:** OK Reddit- FUCK ME UP PLEASE. I'm confined to my bed due to medical issues (I've got a fairly severe spinal fluid leak) and I'm not allowed to sit up, stand up, or walk (other than shorts trips to the bathroom and to get food). I only have an Amazon prime subscription (no Netflix, Hulu, etc ) and am looking for suggestions for things to watch (either movies or series) that will take my mind off of the pain that I'm in and the general shittiness of my quality of life at the moment. 

I'm primarily interested in psychological thrillers, documentaries of almost any kind, suspense and / or horror. 

PLEASE do NOT suggest anything heartwarming, -inducing, or touching / in any way. On top of the medical stuff in also dealing with a broken heart, so I can't handle anything emotional right now. 

I'm also open to comedies (I've got a really dark sense of humor).

I just want something riveting in general. Preferably something that will fuck me up at last to some degree. The more twisted, the better. 

Thank y'all so much for the help! I hope everybody is having a great day. 

TL/DR: I'm bedridden bc of medical issues and need a distraction from this shit (movies or series - I only have Amazon prime). The more unhinged the better. 

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Get well soon… Prince of Darkness (1987)
2. Unfortunately, Prime is overrated. I just had 7 free days of Prime and found very little of worth that was free. The best stuff you still have to pay for. If that’s an option for you, great. However, there are streaming services that are free.

Tubi, Plex, PlutoTV, Fawesome, and others are free with ads. Tubi has a fairly extensive library.

Kanopy and Hoopla are services your library may subscribe to and all you need is a library card. Most libraries allow you to apply for a card online or by phone, especially if they are aware of your physical limitations. Kanopy, especially, has lots of documentaries and films.

If you’re inclined to read, Hoopla also has ebooks and audiobooks. Libby has books and magazines.

Hope recovery is swift and you’re feeling better soon.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Valid Critical Takes on "You Can See Everything"

**Score:** 63
**Body:** There's obviously (and rightfully) a lot of discussion about this movie, but it's almost universally praised as "genius" and "reality bending" and "revolutionary". There are very few critical takes, and most of those aren't taken seriously or are immediately dismissed.

But that puts people in an awkward position: agree with the praise, or be cast as someone who doesn't "get it". There doesn't seem to be any room for, "I understand and appreciate what the movie is trying to do but I question how well it actually does it".

It makes discussing the movie a little frustrating. Criticism is usually met with "you didn't *get it*" or "they did that on purpose!". 

But high concept claims that the movie is *really* about "truth" and "reality" and "subjectivity" aren't actually counterarguments or defenses.

There are legitimate criticisms of how effectively it explores those ideas. Does the ambiguity necessarily reveal something meaningful, or does it simply manufacture uncertainty by intentionally withholding or manipulating context? And if "manufacturing uncertainty" is "the point", then what is the ambiguity actually revealing? Is it just that "sometimes it's hard to know what's true"?

Do the reenactments deepen our understanding or mostly just add a layer of contrived performance?

Does acknowledging its own manipulation automatically make that manipulation more defensible or credible?

Those questions aren’t evidence that someone missed "the point". They’re questions about whether the movie really earns the significance people are attributing to it.

I’m not saying people should enjoy it less. I'm not even saying I didn't enjoy it myself (because I did). I’d just like there to be room to question its effectiveness without having my understanding of it questioned instead.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I don’t think it’s high concept in the sense that it came in with some kind of high concept. imo it’s largely an observational doc & is, if anything, just asking the audience what they see, while essentially admitting that they (the creators) aren’t sure what *they* see. i feel like there’s nothing to “get”. it’s kind of the opposite of that, & if you’re expecting something to get then you might be pretty disappointed. it could feel very unfinished to someone who sees that it’s not really a polished thing with a point, and doesn’t like that
2. I don’t think the film is above criticism or anything, but a lot of the criticisms I have seen are frankly lazy and just not wanting to engage with the film for what it is. That isn’t to say it’s impossible to levy a legitimate criticism towards it, but I’ve seen way too much “is it even a documentary” discussion when it clearly, 100% is. 

I also don’t really mind that it doesn’t say much other than “sometimes it’s hard to know what’s true” as I think that is a valid enough and relevant thesis to have in what often feels like a post-truth world. Above all, I appreciate how slippery and elusive the film is, and have found discussing the motivations of all in the film to be rather fun.

I’m all for a well thought out critique of the film, but I also think to do so one needs to at least attempt to see what the film is trying to accomplish and many of the critiques I’ve seen do seem to fundamentally miss the point. It is not the responsibility of a filmmaker to handhold the viewer to an answer.  
  - Agreed with that first point, but especially the agreed with the second point regarding the scope of its themes. It plays almost more like a narrative mystery such as Burning, with similar preoccupations. 
This is far from what most documentaries do, and it throws people off. I mean, that wrong footing is exactly what makes it so thrilling to those of us who enjoyed it.

I can sympathize with how it annoys people, though. At the end of the day, when I boil the movie down in my head, it’s much less about gaining insight into Holmes and Billy then it is about its own narrative ambitions, with the couple used as sort of fodder to build a narrative. Maybe I’m overstating this, because of course you do learn a lot about the subjects on an emotional level. But if you’re lasers in on the Holmes story, you might find the framing of the film a little absurd — of course she’s psychopathic liar, so why even open the door to “we can never really know” discourse? 

I think that’s a misread of the film, to be clear. The filmmakers expect you to bring external knowledge in (or to find it later). But at the same time…how many people unfamiliar with Holmes now have an unearned image of her as a victim, having only seen the film? I have to admit it’s thorny stuff. It’s part of what makes the movie so bold.
    - I think the idea that she is accountable for her actions legally doesn't supercede the aspects of her life that led her to behave the way she does or how others currently treat her.

The idea she can't be victimized while manipulating others is a fallacy that indivudals perpetuate on their more rigidly oriented criticisms. It's also ambiguous if she is playing a role in her relationship.

Part of the discussion I see from the movie (which is an important discussion in my opinion) is the nature of lies and delusion.

Lies have intent and are known to be false by the liar, delusion is believed and without conscious intent. Part of the point of the movie, although self serving in his style of media (and why people find it interesting to backpack on the idea of the social issue of post truth era) is the question of how much of what Holmes says is a lie? It remains up for interpretation and the point is we (her) may not know or allow others to know.

How does someone get here? What is their life like and who are they surrounded by? What is the nature of her intention?

I for one enjoy the philosophizing and ambiguity as it points to larger questions that we should consider. The world is not all black and white as much as we want it to be.
3. I think part of what's so interesting and refreshing about this film is that Nathan does everything a documentarian does, and he does it well, and he invests so much into it, and you can tell that he wants to find the answer really bad up until the very end. Documentaries want to come to a point: they want to say something. He clearly did too. But he failed. And he certainly could have just ran with something at several points, but he didn't. Instead of scrapping the film, he reframed the entire thing, saw the beauty in the journey, and said "here, you can see everything too". It was a documentary, but then it became a meta-documentary because Nathan became a character.

Now, it would feel dishonest if Nathan planned all along to have it end like this with this uncertainty, and I think that would be a devastating point of criticism if it were true. So I'm not rejecting the concept of film criticism. 

I just find film criticism uninteresting often because I think it must come from a place of love almost to be effective. Because you need to form a conclusion about what the film is trying to be and that requires a little bit of thought and watching the movie once with a truly open mind and just letting it be what it wants to be. In this film's case you literally do not know what this film is trying to be until the very end, and if you formed a conclusion at any other point you would be wrong. 

I think this film is at its core, trying to be honest through and through: you can see everything. So if you found how it's dishonest and made a compelling argument for why, I'd call that criticism compelling. Moreso, it would actually change my whole perspective of the movie. But when the criticism is that it paints this horrible person in a positive light, or it gives her all these excuses, or it's not credibly telling the story of Elizabeth Holmes, it's just missing the point.

Also too many people watch films with the desire to form criticisms, or just create talking points to have discussions with friends afterward and because of that, they don't let the movie take them for a ride. IMO you really have to do your best to let the movie be something fun and enjoyable, and genuinely try to love it, before you criticize it, and most people don't do that. Criticism from someone you love is always the most devastating. It's the same with media.

As for the film itself, it's refreshing to me because it defies black and white thinking, denies the satisfaction of a conclusion about who is good or bad. It's just human and that's what we all are at the end of the day. Is Elizabeth Holmes truly earnest and governed by motivated reasoning? Or is she a sociopath and knows exactly what she's doing?

I have a theory that Elizabeth Holmes and Billy Evans are both engaging in a form of motivated reasoning where one covers the gaps left by the other, unconsciously and instinctively filling in each others' roles in order to fulfill the vision. Billy truly believes in Elizabeth and she truly believes in him. They are both fooling each other as they do everyone else but they also complement each other.

Could be a stupid theory but that this is all left open for us to ponder despite seeing so much is a testament to the mosaic that people are and how silly it is to demand simple explanations for everything. 

I will say one black-and-white takeaway I got was just how vulnerable society is to entrepreneurs. Holmes' affect reminded me a lot of Mark Zuckerburg tbh, and made me think about all these other billionaires and con-men that get away with so much in our society. Painting these folks as merely human makes me look at the systems that enable them. It's truly on society at large that we get fooled by these pretenders instead of listening to actual scientists, or at the very least solicit the aid of scientists to question them.
4. As someone who works professionally with people who lie and manipulate as well as are delusional, I found the central question, or the idea of there being ambiguity, about Holmes' duplicity uninteresting. Because its not a compelling question to me--of course she is duplicitous, manipulative, and in a perhaps smaller than those measure, self-delusive. I came away from the film a little disappointed because I thought it would give us insight into that kind of mind, which again, I have experience with, and which in this case was highly successful for some time, but instead it presented as ambiguous something I think in truth is a lot less so. Also, the most interesting parts for me, such as the interaction with the dad, were curtailed rather than explored. I also think the response to it as pure genius is starting to be a little weird because while a fun film, while engaging and expertly done, and in some cases quite funny and interesting, it doesn't seem close to a masterpiece to me. Maybe if I hadn't had those expectations, as much as I tried to ignore them, coming in, I wouldn't have been as disappointed.
5. I think part of the reason the movie feels “critique proof” is that it’s kind of poking fun at the audience for constantly trying to find a deeper meaning. While yes, the movie is showing how many filters “the truth” goes through in art and documentary, basically the ending shows that Elizabeth was the same manipulative liar we all thought she was (she knew about money deal all along). We could in fact see everything; but, like Nathan, the more we try to find some core reason or deeper truth to the Theranos story, the more we look like fools. 
6. I think this is a good general rule for every film discussion. No movie is above criticism or beneath praise. Opinions are subjective, that’s why they’re opinions. And you’re right, there is a very unfortunate tendency in this age of social media righteousness to dismiss opinions that aren’t your own not as opposing but as out-and-out objectively wrong. This has always been a problem, but with *Digger* and *You Can See Everything* this year, the polarization seems especially personal, and it seems to be contagious to discourse on other movies.
  - I want to piggyback off you here a bit because you already said most of what I might have said but you raise a more interesting point , which is the way people discuss their opinions of media as if they are competing realities rather than differing perspectives. It is entirely valid for someone to believe this movie is genius and reality bending and revolutionary and someone else to view it as, say for example, try hard or contrived. And neither of those views are wrong even if they appear to be opposed to each other because no one, not even a panel of experts has The Only True Lens of Reality. We all only see the world through our experience. Expert consensus of Monet's time almost entirely disregarded his technique and method as amateur , incomplete and even ugly. And they would be laughed at today for saying that but these were THE experts of the time. So who was right? Is there such a thing? I don't think so
    - Not to be the “people are uneducated” guy, but I’m very concerned about … well, people being uneducated. Folks these days, especially younger folks, legitimately do not seem to know the difference between fact and opinion, and the notion that something can be true for them and untrue for someone else or vice versa seems to blow their minds. This has all kinds of horrifying implications for issues beyond arts criticism. If you can’t accept the possibility that someone may have a different set of beliefs than you and that those beliefs are valid when it comes to *movies*, how are you going to do it when it comes to religion or sexuality or whatever?

## 4. Wildwood (2026) not going to save us. A billionaire is not capable of creating "Art in its purest form." Has our culture forgotten what art actually is?

**Score:** 0
**Body:** (preface)  
I wrestled with the film Wildwood and wrote this essay for myself. I went to post it and was greeted by outside information that clarified many of the answers I had arrived at when working through the film on its own. Then came an epilogue of eureka and glee. I believe this encapsulates why self-reflection is an essential aspect of consuming art and I encourage others to wrestle themselves if we are to survive the coming age.

(the original essay)  
Wildwood depressed me. For some reason each step I have taken afterwards has been accompanied by distant screams from within. The voices cry out behind my eyes, “Cast it out so it does not take root!” Thus:

A beautifully crafted hollow image is the most painful to watch. It wasn’t that I didn’t “agree” with everything that happened. I did. I get the movie. It is about the climate catastrophe and the older generation sacrificing the younger generation because of their outdated beliefs. It is about seeing magic in a rationalist world that stops the young from venturing into the unknown. It is about duty and fighting for what you believe in. It is about the fear of death. It is an updated Chronicles of Narnia, where Aslan is an Eagle and Christianity has been exchanged for liberal plant worship.

There was something distressingly inhuman about it, even though it screamed “humanity” constantly at its audience. When you watch it, it wants you to think it is good. Look at how much “art” happened! “It was crafted by human hands! Thousands and thousands of human hands! It was not made by a machine!”

I fear that this is a harbinger of liberal humanist battlegrounds for the coming fight against AI. They think we need to recruit human bodies to form the machine. I.e. a 21st century John Henry. It is a cruel misunderstanding of what art is. Art is never in the labor. Labor is necessary to realize a vision, but if labor is spent realizing something hollow and inhuman, that labor was simply work, not art. If this is the ground we choose to fight on, we will have lost before the battle even begins.

(Unfortunately a majority of the film’s most popular reviews occupy this ground – “the biggest middle finger to generative AI of all time.”)

This film is a contemporary pyramid. In truth, we have never stopped building the pyramids. Our culture is just as obsessed with religious temples as any that has come before, we just have different gods. Films and media are the temples of our time. The religious epicenter of any culture is simply whatever art people care about and engage with. We have exchanged religious services for media consumption, but we are still human. We can still feel truth and belief in the poetic genius when we see it, and we, like every other culture, seek to enshrine and pass down works that testify to where the human condition can reach towards at a given moment.

However, we have entered an era of objectivity. Where the thing must be “good” because it has been quantified as “good” based on empirical evidence. We assess our art as scientists and think the greatest works have the most “art” inside of them. For example, “Each frame of this movie has more “art” than that other movie.” This gets us in an inhuman situation where we forced ourselves to think that the temple must hold a god, because it is objectively “valuable” and formalisticly “beautiful.”

Think of someone in ancient Egypt. How would it feel for this individual to enter that pyramid that had been touched and cared for by all of their community? What if when they stood at the center, they were confronted, not with a god, but by the empty and cruel vanity of man. Standing inside that ornate monument, should this individual justify the pharaoh’s divinity simply because of the amount of death and toil which constructed his magnificent temple? Is it disrespectful to the slaves that gave their lives to build it, to observe something hollow at its center? And is it disrespectful to the slaves that gave their lives to build it, to seek for the pyramid to be torn down?

To the ground. We must destroy our beautiful empty temples no matter how uncomfortable this makes us feel. How can I justify this review to the laborers who spent years of their lives building this film? I can do it by arguing that the alternative is much worse. If we are to survive the coming age, we must be unafraid to reveal what makes us human. We must gather around works of art that do not reflect the vague systematic notion of humanity but works of art that could ONLY be created by a living breathing human being. This film uses labor and technology directed towards an objective surface level – the level of the filmic image. Despite the warnings of the AI bell tollers, we will always “win” against what we have created because the human condition is indescribable. Even words are the fumbling afterthought of something long dead inside our souls. As subjective creatures, we can never be “replaced” because what makes us human cannot be manifest, only hinted at. However, we can be replaced if our battle rests at the objective surface level. We must never forget that our images are nothing without their source, no matter how laborious or formally technical that image might be. We must not worship labor and efficiency because this is the language of capitalism not art.

This film is more like patronage than art. Attempting to artificially realize a “consensus.” Patronage is wanting the world to be thought of a certain way and having the resources to make a mass amount of people see the world in this way. This is the logic of Pharaohs. Winning over the mass, not by touching their soul and shaping what they believe, but by constructing the worlds they are forced to perceive. I fear this film thinks art is just a fake version of the “real” world -- "the real world should become like this fake world because of how beautiful and expensive it was to craft."

This is not acceptable. We must feel the human breath in our art. Create something that is unique to yourself. We are subjective beings. I felt the objectivity of this world in every frame. All the hands on the clay, and all the hands on the writing, all the hands on it. Just too many hands. It is too much. How can any human cry out in this ornate world where the bar to be "heard" is placed beyond the capabilities of the individual? This is not saving us from the machine; this is fighting the machine on its terms. The communal artistic language of the species is slowly being moved beyond the capabilities of the individual artist, into a world of mass toil and expensive technology. And once that happens, we will find ourselves trapped in a fake world unable to cry out.

How painfully this irony slips through the fingers of this film’s makers. The film is about sacrificing the “individual” innocent in an attempt to create a fake version of life. It wears the costume of the savior while it itself holds the knife. This objective quantification art traps our culture’s most vulnerable in a simulation world of beautiful inhuman images and the inability to change them unless they become machines themselves. We are not meant to be willing cogs in an artistic machine. What the hell is happening. Can no one see the insanity of this statement?

I have probably been too hard on this film in particular. It is just painful to watch something that claims it is freeing the young while actively building chains to ensnare them. It was screaming at me to praise it, but the more it screamed at me, the more I wept.

(epilogue)  
IT COULD NOT HAVE BEEN WRITTEN! THIS MOVIE WAS MADE BY A BILLIONAIRE! I KNEW IT THE WHOLE TIME. It speaks the language of money. I felt it in every frame. It is SUCH a billionaire movie. They are surrounded by formalistic beauty with empty empty teeny tiny souls. HAHAHA. Of course this man thinks art is as many little hands as possible endlessly laboring over his own bland stupid vision. CAPITALISM AS ART HAHA! And we praise it! How about we stop letting vampires tell us about the human condition. I SAID it was a pyramid without knowing any of this. We are all in the pyramid and we praise the Pharaoh for his slave labor! Haha! It is even funnier because it is NIKE who literally uses slave labor. These people are parasites who don’t want to stop sucking but don’t want to feel bad about it. They fund these vanity projects as sleeping pills. The landed gentry want to play artist so they build the fanciest prettiest most expensive stage hahahaha! They are combining technology and art, so only they have the tools to play! They will never win on fair terms so they change the rules! They feel nothing and they think the problem is that the images they look at are not constructed well enough.

How did I read all of this just from watching the film by itself? My soul immediately cried out in pain after consuming something empty. I am sure many of these 5-star reviewers felt the emptiness as well but rationally justified their praise because they want to appear as "pro-art." This whole thing is just like Jessie Plemmons at the end of Digger. That is scary. Wow. What a fun night. This is why you engage with art yourself instead of treating it like a science. Look at how many volunteer to guard an empty temple! HAHA! If you guard something you never have to look inside! We love the pharaohs and want to keep building their temples! According to these comments, Billionaires are the only ones capable of creating "Art in its purest form!" Our lives are really just an extension of theirs! This is what happens when god dies – the men with power move into the temple. Then humanity has toil without even the chance at salvation. And guess what this film tells us – our toil IS our salvation! HAHAHA! AMAZING! And we praise it

You can tell how scared he is based on how beautifully he made each frame. He has meticulously curated his outside to compensate for the chasm that is his inside. If you have something you want people to listen to, stick your neck out. That is what an actual human artist does. This man has hidden himself inside of precisely what our culture is afraid of attacking -- artistic labor. Come out of the dark and look your laborers in the eyes. See how it feels to tell them what you are actually doing, "Your toil for my temple is your only chance at salvation. If you want material art to survive, I am your savior. Your lives and labor are nothing but a costume I wear to seek love from others without having to change myself." Something tells me they won't find it as convincing when coming from your lips.  
\- Written 25 October 2026
